core.text: The subjunctive can also soften a statement into a possibility: **the potential subjunctive (the 'could / would / may' form: velim = I would like)**. *Tē adiuvem* — I could help you; *aliquis dīcat* — someone might say; *fortasse veniam* — I may come. Its commonest use is polite: *velim* — I would like; *nōlim* — I would rather not; *mālim* — I would prefer. Latin name: *coniūnctīvus potentiālis*.
English does the same with *would*, *could*, *might*: *I would like to come*, *one might say*.
Present (or perfect) subjunctive in a main clause, often with aliquis, quis or fortasse: 'could / would / may'. Negative nōn.

invented.en: I would like to come, but I can't.
Someone might say: 'I don't believe it.'

core.text: Same form, different tone: **the subjunctive as a wish or gentle command (eamus = let's go; veniat = let him come)** wants something to happen (*veniat* — let him come); the potential only says it could (*veniat* — he may come). Wishes take *nē*, possibilities *nōn*; *fortasse* or *aliquis* points to the potential.

more.text: The learner's notes (week 27) call it possibility or probability, 'often used merely to weaken a statement in order to be polite', and single out *possim, velim, nōlim, mālim*: *venīre possim* — I could come; *venīre velim* — I would like to come.

With the imperfect subjunctive the possibility moves into the past or becomes unreal: *vellem* — I would wish (but it cannot be); *dīcerēs* — you would have said. The perfect subjunctive is common in cautious statements: *haud sciō an ita dīxerim* — I rather think I said so. In the second person it is the general 'you': *crēdās* — one would believe.
Nothing has been wished for and nobody has been told anything: the speaker is holding the idea out at arm's length.
Latin reaches for *velim* and *nōlim* exactly where English softens 'I want' into 'I would like'.

*Quis haec verba vēra esse crēdat?* is 'who would believe these words are true?', not 'who believes them?'. When one of these stands next to a subjunctive in a main clause (the sentence's own verb, not one tucked inside another clause), read 'could', 'might' or 'would'.

The negative is the test that separates the two main-clause uses, wish and possibility: the same verb in the same person, and the negative is the whole difference. Look at which negative is standing there before you decide which reading the sentence wants.
Put the right person on the subjunctive stem (what is left of the verb before the ending) and let the rest of the sentence do the softening.

teach.title: A verb that only says 'could'

notice.ask: Which word in each sentence says something that could happen, not something that does?

teach.say: The present subjunctive can let go of its force and say only that something is possible: **the potential subjunctive (the 'could / would / may' form: velim = I would like)**. *Tē iuvāre possim* is not 'let me help you' but 'I could help you'.

check.ask: Does possīs say that you can do it, or that you could?

teach.title: velim and nōlim: the polite ones
teach.say: The commonest potentials are the verbs of wanting: **velim** 'I would like', **nōlim** 'I would rather not' — the present subjunctive of *volō* and *nōlō*, with the ordinary **-m** of the 'I' person on the subjunctive stem (what is left of the verb before the ending) *veli-* / *nōli-*.

check.ask: Fill the blank with the form of volō that means 'I would like'.

teach.title: The words that point at it
teach.say: Latin usually sets a word beside the verb that points at the possibility: *fortasse* 'perhaps', *aliquis* 'someone', *nēmō* 'nobody', or a question with *quis* 'who'. *Aliquis dīcat* is 'someone might say' — an imagined speaker, not one who has spoken.

teach.title: The negative is nōn
teach.say: A wish or command is denied with *nē*; a possibility is denied with **nōn**: *nōn crēdās*, 'you would not believe'. So *nē crēdās* forbids you to believe, while *nōn crēdās* only doubts.

check.ask: What is crēdat doing here — wishing for it, or saying it could happen?

teach.title: Using it in any person
teach.say: The potential is not only for 'I': *intellegās* 'you could understand', *emat* 'he would buy', *ferat* 'he could carry' — the ordinary present subjunctive endings, and the sense stays 'could / would'.

check.ask: Fill the blank with the form of volō that means 'would want'.
